st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central distinction between increased participation and effective remedies, and materially develops it with complaint-level outcome evidence, a mechanism of displaced pre-filing screening, and a court-side reform agenda designed to preserve access while restoring screening, comprehension and solicitude.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The source accepts that AI-assisted filings remain the signer’s responsibility and that genuine citations can still misstate or fail to support the law. It materially extends the cluster by identifying an access-to-justice problem: unrepresented litigants may be legally incapable of performing meaningful verification even when no authority is fabricated, making certification a potential trap or formality.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s distinction between nominal human accountability and effective control: a pro se litigant may sign and know the grievance without authoring or understanding the AI-generated legal text. It materially extends the synthesis by showing how this mismatch disrupts court screening and procedural protections, and by proposing function-focused safeguards rather than disclosure or prohibition alone.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central account that AI can expand formal access without improving remedies and can shift screening burdens onto courts and defendants. It materially extends that proposition by identifying doctrinal mechanisms—especially disrupted assumptions about human authorship and the “polish penalty”—and proposing function-centric institutional repair rather than prohibition.
qs: The  emerging proposals regulate the use of the tool; this Article shows why that cannot work, and  builds the alternative: a function-centric program that rebuilds screening, comprehension, and  solicitude on the court’s side without withdrawing the access AI has produced.44           The Article proceeds in five Parts.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s distinction between expanded AI-enabled assistance and improved access to justice, and materially develops it with complaint-level evidence that polished AI-associated filings achieve no better outcomes. It further identifies a concrete workflow consequence: front-end screening costs are displaced from lawyers to courts, staff and defendants.
qs: This is the litigation-efficacy paradox: more entry, more legal form, but no greater access to remedy.
The screening that AI displaces does not disappear; it migrates to the docket, burdening judges, staff, and defendants.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s implementation-focused concern that apparent access gains do not establish reliable legal-service delivery, and materially extends it with a doctrinal account of shifted screening costs and the “polish penalty.” It shows how AI-generated legal form can burden courts and defendants while causing procedural protections for untrained litigants to misfire.
qs: The deepest misfire is the polish penalty: the solicitude the law reserves for the  untrained is withdrawn from the untrained litigant because generative AI has made her filing read  as though it were trained.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s selective-deployment and work-redesign proposition, then materially extends it with associational federal-court evidence that AI may increase pro se entry without improving remedies. It proposes a concrete division of labour: automate ministerial intake while reserving consequential screening and judgment for humans and avoiding rubber-stamp review.

st.t: Effective help: Justice outcomes outrank lawyer supply
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s outcome-focused framing by identifying why lawyer supply and formal self-representation alone do not ensure effective access: contingency-fee incentives screen out lower-value claims, while lawyer-oriented procedures disadvantage unrepresented litigants. It does not assess comparative justice outcomes or substantiate an AI solution.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central account that human signers remain accountable for AI-assisted filings and that verification extends beyond detecting fabricated citations. It particularly reinforces the access-to-justice tension: self-represented litigants remain subject to reasonable-inquiry duties despite often lacking the expertise to assess genuine authorities or legal theories. Although it reports several regulatory proposals, it does not clearly endorse a competing governance model.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that responsibility for accurate filings remains with human litigants, whether represented or self-represented. st.t: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis: it documents a substantial post-ChatGPT rise in federal self-representation while expressly limiting the evidence to association, finds no improvement in per-case success for AI-flagged complaints, and argues that cheaper drafting may relocate screening costs to courts and defendants. Its court-side reform proposals preserve access while acknowledging that their benefits remain testable predictions.

kp.k: Court access and access to remedy are distinct
kp.d: Cohen-Sasson distinguishes producing and docketing a complaint from obtaining lawful relief. The paper argues that generative AI expands the former without demonstrated improvement in per-case outcomes. It nevertheless recognizes participation and being heard as independent dignitary goods, and explicitly allows that more filings could increase the absolute number of favorable outcomes even without higher success rates.
qs: The two are different, and a system can supply the first without supplying the second.
This claim addresses the rate of relief. Due to the pro se surge, the absolute number of favorable outcomes may rise while per-case success has not risen.

kp.k: Federal self-representation accelerated after public generative AI access
kp.d: The filing-level analysis covers approximately 2.8 million federal civil filings in FY2008–FY2025, excluding prisoner petitions and unknown case types. The plaintiff pro se rate increased from 11.33% before the November 30, 2022 cutoff to 16.94% afterward, reaching 22.30% in FY2025-Q4. Annual trends were +0.078 percentage points before and +2.996 afterward; interrupted time-series models show acceleration rather than a statistically significant immediate level shift. District, case-category and COVID controls do not eliminate the association, but the paper expressly disclaims causal identification.
qs: Across all federal civil filings, the plaintiff pro se rate rose from 11.33% before the GenAI cutoff to 16.94% after it.
These models do not establish that generative AI caused the surge; no observational design could.

kp.k: The surge appears substantially additive, not simple lawyer substitution
kp.d: Average quarterly pro se filings increased 54.7%, from 4,152 to 6,423, while represented filings declined from 31,654 to 30,637. Total quarterly civil filings increased 2.9%, from 36,697 to 37,765. The author interprets the pro se increase exceeding twice the represented decline as inconsistent with one-for-one substitution of self-representation for legal labor, while allowing partial displacement.
qs: The pro se increase is more than double the size of the represented decline, and average quarterly civil filings rose overall.

Whatever displacement of represented litigation occurred was partial, not one-to-one, and the pro se surge appears substantially additive, a distinction that bears on the debate over whether AI substitutes for legal labor.

kp.k: Changes vary substantially across legal fields
kp.d: Civil Rights pro se rates increased from 28.16% to 35.60%, and Other Statutory rates from 11.23% to 19.51%. These focal categories comprise roughly 36.7% of the all-civil docket and anchor the complaint-level analysis. Real Property, Torts, Tax and Contract also increased; Forfeiture/Penalty, Labor and Intellectual Property were comparatively flat, while Social Security and Immigration declined. The author treats stakes, specialization and counsel availability as possible explanations rather than established mechanisms.
qs: The unevenness itself is informative, cautioning against any account on which generative AI uniformly transforms civil litigation.
Differences in stakes, in legal specialization, and in the practical availability of counsel could be relevant factors that shape this pattern.

kp.k: Textual flags measure AI-consistent drafting, not verified use
kp.d: The complaint corpus comprises 12,842 pro se complaints from FY2018–FY2025, collected through CourtListener; 12,451, or 97.0%, were matched to IDB records. A classifier combines sentence-length uniformity, LLM-favored vocabulary and lexical diversity, with thresholds calibrated against pre-cutoff complaints. It identifies a net 13.9% of post-AI freely drafted focal-category complaints, versus 9.8% including templates and 4.3% among templates alone. Validation includes adoption-proxy correlations, component movements and co-occurrence, and threshold robustness. The author characterizes this as a conservative measure of visible drafting assistance, not a census of all AI help or proof of individual use.
qs: Nothing in this design identifies direct use of generative AI by a particular plaintiff.
The AI-flagged subset is therefore best understood as a conservative slice of AI-touched litigation, not a census of it.

kp.k: More legal form accompanies worse observed litigation trajectories
kp.d: AI-flagged freely drafted complaints have median citation density of 6.01 per thousand words, compared with 4.40 for unflagged post-AI complaints and 3.98 before AI. Among concluded post-AI cases, dismissal rates are 61.1% versus 53.6%, and termination before an answer is 47.8% versus 39.0%. Plaintiff win rates are 6.4% versus 8.4%, a statistically insignificant difference. The author calls this the litigation-efficacy paradox and emphasizes that citations measure form, not legal quality.
qs: Citation density is not a measure of legal quality.
AI-flagged complaints tend to be more formal, yet they fare no better overall, and on dismissal and early termination, worse.

kp.k: Outcome evidence is limited to concluded, observed cases
kp.d: The dismissal and early-termination analysis includes 3,924 cases terminated by the observation cutoff; many post-AI cases remain pending. The dismissal gap has p = 0.006 and the early-termination gap p = 0.002. The win comparison uses plaintiff judgments over plaintiff-plus-defendant judgments with clear coding, comprising 47 flagged and 333 unflagged cases, with p = 0.635. The paper treats these as revisable trajectories, not final outcomes for all filings, and does not empirically apportion the dismissal gap among claim selection, output defects and judicial treatment.
qs: these figures are best read as trajectories of concluded cases, re-estimable as the window lengthens.
The share of the dismissal gap attributable to relocated screening rather than a genuine merits deficit is an empirical question.

kp.k: AI-consistent drafting disproportionately accompanies newly observed plaintiffs
kp.d: Within the post-AI sample, 79.4% of flagged complaints involve first-time observed plaintiffs versus 70.2% of unflagged complaints, with odds ratio 1.638 and p < 0.001. First-time means the first observed primary-plaintiff name in the FY2018–FY2025 identity-linked sample, not verified lifetime litigation history. The finding challenges accounts centering the surge on serial litigants. Name-inferred female shares are 19.7% versus 15.0%, but the paper treats that signal as tentative because it relies on inference and p = 0.051.
qs: AI-consistent drafting is disproportionately the work of plaintiffs the docket had not seen before.
“first-time” means the first observed appearance of the primary plaintiff’s name in the fiscal 2018–2025 identity-linked sample.

kp.k: Expanded drafting capacity does not reach everyone equally
kp.d: Fee-waiver status, the paper's proxy for financial constraint, occurs in 27.3% of flagged versus 24.4% of unflagged complaints, not a significant difference (p = 0.12). Across the pro se docket, fee-waiver rates fell from 42.3% to 35.9% after the cutoff. The author concludes that the surge is not concentrated among the financially neediest. Circuit flag rates also vary significantly, but comparisons are unadjusted for population or docket composition and cannot establish the sources of geographic variation.
qs: But it is not concentrated among the financially neediest.
Lowering the cost of producing a complaint, it turns out, does not distribute the new capacity equally.

kp.k: AI weakens two different pre-filing filters
kp.d: The author distinguishes drafting friction, which screens by capacity rather than merit, from lawyer consultation, which screens partly through professional judgment. Near-zero-cost drafting removes the former; reliance on chatbots can displace the latter. The paper qualifies the historical comparison: lawyer selection also reflects expected recovery, ability to pay and risk, can reject meritorious claims, and reaches only people able to obtain consultation. Consequently, removing friction alone predicts more filings but does not explain the flagged subset's worse outcomes.
qs: The feature of the drafting friction filter is that it screens by capacity rather than by merit.
The professional-judgment filter was never purely a merits screen.
Fluency, like friction, is blind to merit.

kp.k: Sycophantic advice may replace lawyers' candid discouragement
kp.d: Cohen-Sasson proposes that chatbot validation can invert the lawyer's gatekeeping function: cheap drafting and encouragement make marginal claims more attractive to file. The mechanism draws on sycophancy research, professional duties of candid advice and OpenAI's April 2025 rollback, with explicit recognition that sycophancy varies by model and context. Nippon Life v. OpenAI is presented as allegations in pending litigation, not established evidence that ChatGPT caused the claimant's conduct.
qs: LLMs exhibit sycophancy, a systematic tendency to agree with, validate, and elaborate the user’s stated beliefs, even at the expense of accuracy.
These are allegations in pending litigation, but their structure is the point.

kp.k: Screening work migrates from private consultations to public dockets
kp.d: The paper argues that screening does not disappear: judges, court staff and defendants bear work previously performed privately through drafting barriers and lawyer declinations. In forma pauperis cases face statutory pre-service review; fee-paid cases ordinarily require service and a defendant's challenge, subject to jurisdictional and narrow frivolousness exceptions. Public screening requires reasoned, reviewable orders rather than informal refusal, while courts cannot simply decline jurisdiction. The author recognizes that this added burden also purchases meaningful participation and explanation for litigants.
qs: What changes is where the sorting happens, who performs it, and who pays.
A lawyer’s screening ends in a sentence. A declination needs no reasons, record, or review. A court’s screening ends in an order, reasons stated, on a public record, subject to appeal.

kp.k: Professional regulation lacks an equivalent pre-filing AI gatekeeper
kp.d: The author argues that licensing, professional conduct duties, malpractice exposure and contingency incentives normally support lawyer screening but do not map reliably onto a chatbot-assisted layperson. Rule 11 still binds unrepresented signers; § 1927 generally does not reach non-attorney pro se litigants, while bad-faith sanctions and filing injunctions remain exceptional safeguards. Providers lack the ordinary attorney-client duty, and software-focused unauthorized-practice enforcement is characterized as contested and rare. Arizona and Utah reforms further complicate reliance on traditional professional boundaries.
qs: The provider stands in no attorney-client relationship with the litigant and owes, under current law, no duty of professional competence.
They are at once contested and dormant.

kp.k: Machine drafting separates signer, factual witness and author
kp.d: The doctrinal argument identifies a shared implicit premise behind plausibility pleading, Rule 11 and liberal construction: the pro se signer also knows the facts and composed the text. Adopting machine-written prose separates those roles without transferring knowledge or accountability to the model. This argument targets direct adoption of output, not all AI use; the author says it weakens where litigants learn from AI and draft with understanding.
qs: She is the signer, who stands behind the document and is accountable for it; she is the witness, the source of the factual narrative because she lived it; and she is the author, who chose the words on the page.
The argument recedes as comprehension grows.

kp.k: Doctrinal fluency cannot replace a plausible factual narrative
kp.d: Under Twombly and Iqbal, factual specificity matters while legal conclusions and formulaic elements are discounted. The author argues that models can supply abundant doctrinal language and citations without the dated, situated facts only the litigant can provide. Validation-oriented interaction may elaborate legal framing rather than elicit missing facts. Citation-density and dismissal associations fit this account, but do not separately prove it.
qs: The model does not know those facts unless the litigant supplies them in detail, and the conversational dynamic works against their development.
The AI-assisted complaint is therefore liable to be rich in what Iqbal discards and thin in what Iqbal requires.

kp.k: Rule 11 exposes comprehension and verification gaps
kp.d: The paper reports courts enforcing reasonable inquiry against AI-assisted pro se signers, including for fabricated citations. Its broader argument is that verification requires more than confirming a case exists: laypeople may be unable to assess whether real authority supports a proposition or whether a theory is sound. The author characterizes uncomprehending certification as potentially either a sanctions trap or an empty formality, while acknowledging that this routine comprehension problem lacks the visible docket evidence supplied by fabricated citations.
qs: Generative AI severs comprehension from signature.
The reasonable-inquiry standard assumes a signer capable of the inquiry; the AI-assisted layperson is asked to certify content she is structurally unequipped to vet.

kp.k: The polish penalty is a prediction, not established finding
kp.d: Drawing on attorney-ghostwriting and lawyer-pro-se cases, Cohen-Sasson predicts that professional-looking machine prose could lead courts to withhold liberal construction despite the litigant's unchanged lack of training. The paper frames this as a protective doctrine potentially reversing its operation when polish stops signaling competence. Critically, it acknowledges no published federal decision withholding liberal construction simply because a pro se complaint reads too well; this mechanism is not demonstrated by the outcome data.
qs: No published federal decision has yet withheld liberal construction from a pro se complaint on the ground that it reads too well.

The pure form of the polish penalty, i.e., solicitude lost not because the filing is flawed (e.g., by hallucinated citations) but because it reads as competent professional work, is therefore a prediction the doctrine’s logic entails.

kp.k: Reform should restore functions rather than prohibit tools
kp.d: The author rejects disclosure, verification certifications and bans as sufficient repairs for lost judgment, comprehension and solicitude, arguing that prohibition would withdraw accessible assistance from already underserved litigants. The recommended approach targets disrupted functions. It leaves room for sanctions against intentional fabricated authority and for provider duties aimed at reducing legal-help sycophancy, although the paper does not design or specify enforcement of such provider duties.
qs: A disclosure form discloses the tool but restores none of those functions.
Such a duty is function-centric notwithstanding that it reaches the provider.

kp.k: AI-aware forms could channel drafting toward legally operative facts
kp.d: The proposed redesign of existing court forms asks who did what, when and where, what harm resulted, jurisdiction, relief and procedural prerequisites. The author predicts that widely adopted official forms could guide both litigants and models, surface recurring defects earlier and signal unrepresented status despite polished prose. These are proposed benefits, not evaluated results.
qs: The court cannot control the tool, but it can control the document architecture the tool must complete
A complaint filed on a court template announces the litigant’s unrepresented standing on its face, restoring the cue that AI’s polish erodes, and so blunting the polish penalty before it can operate.

kp.k: Automate ministerial intake while reserving adverse judgment for humans
kp.d: Court-side AI would check completeness, classify and route filings, using objective ministerial rather than predicted-merits escalation criteria. Human reviewers would receive no machine merits verdict to reduce automation bias. The author grounds human control over denial in dignity and legitimacy, not only current model limitations, and preserves Rule 5(d)(4)'s restriction on refusing papers solely for defective form.
qs: the machine may clear and route, but only a human may turn a litigant away.
The reason to reserve the decision is not necessarily the machine’s incapacity but the character of the decision.

kp.k: New public-facing roles could restore candid legal judgment
kp.d: The paper predicts expansion of pro se staff attorneys, magistrate-judge screening and self-help centers, alongside intake evaluators and AI-oriented legal aid. It proposes adapting early neutral evaluation into an advisory front door that supplies candid strengths-and-weaknesses assessment without imposing an outcome. For fee-paid litigants, this must operate through advice rather than a new coercive merits screen. These roles reflect a societal choice to reserve judgment for humans, not necessarily human technical superiority.
qs: new human roles created not necessarily because the machine cannot perform the task but because society declines to let it.
The front door is built for that majority because it operates by candor, not command.

kp.k: Solicitude should follow lay status rather than document polish
kp.d: The author recommends applying liberal construction based on the litigant's unrepresented standing and lack of training rather than textual sophistication. This is an interpretive adjustment, not relaxation of plausibility or a subsidy for meritless claims. The proposed repair aims to protect meritorious machine-polished complaints from treatment premised on lawyer competence.
qs: A court should extend liberal construction on the basis of the litigant’s unrepresented standing, which is a matter of record, not on the basis of how the filing reads, which a tool can now counterfeit.
It is an interpretive posture, not a merits subsidy.

kp.k: Reforms require resources and multi-measure evaluation
kp.d: The paper describes interpretive recalibration as nearly costless and ministerial automation as potentially freeing staff capacity, but acknowledges that expanded human evaluation and legal aid require investment. Proposed evaluation tracks dismissal and amendment rates, jurisdictional defects, want-of-prosecution terminations, pre-filing abandonment and outcome composition. These are predicted effects rather than measured reform results; lower dismissal rates alone cannot distinguish improved access from weaker screening, and right-censoring remains relevant.
qs: The investment-dependent piece is the new and expanded human roles—the intake evaluators, the front door, the AI-oriented legal aid—which require real resources.

A falling dismissal rate, standing alone, cannot distinguish reforms that work from screening that has merely grown lax; the rate must be interpreted alongside amendment rates, win rates, and the right-censoring caveat.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Cohen-Sasson argues that generative AI expands access to filing lawsuits without demonstrating improved per-case access to remedies, and relocates screening and human judgment into courts.
pts.d: The author reports an accelerating increase in federal civil self-representation after ChatGPT's release, from a pre-cutoff share of 11.33% to 22.30% in FY2025-Q4. He characterizes the increase as substantially additive rather than a one-for-one replacement of represented litigation. His 'litigation-efficacy paradox' is that AI-flagged complaints have more legal form, measured by citation density, but higher dismissal and early-termination rates and no statistically significant plaintiff-win advantage. He proposes two explanations: AI reduces drafting friction and replaces candid lawyer screening with potentially validating chatbot advice; and machine authorship separates the signer from the composer, undermining procedural assumptions about factual grounding, comprehension, and legal competence. His 'polish penalty' predicts that professional-looking AI prose can deprive an untrained litigant of liberal construction. His proposed response combines AI-aware forms, automated ministerial intake, human-only adverse screening decisions, candid neutral evaluation, and solicitude based on litigant status rather than prose sophistication. He predicts these changes could reduce defective filings, preserve meritorious claims, and expand public-facing human screening roles rather than eliminate human work.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines observational filing and complaint data with doctrinal analysis, adjacent AI research, and illustrative litigation; it expressly distinguishes the predicted polish penalty from directly observed findings.
pts.d: The filing analysis uses approximately 2.8 million Federal Judicial Center records for FY2008–FY2025, excluding prisoner petitions and unknown case types. The complaint corpus comprises 12,842 pro se complaints from FY2018–FY2025, collected through CourtListener; 12,451 were linked to case records. AI flags combine sentence-length uniformity, AI-associated vocabulary, and lexical diversity, calibrated against pre-release complaints. Validation includes adoption-proxy correlations, component convergence, and threshold robustness. The net flag estimate is 13.9% in freely drafted complaints in the focal Civil Rights and Other Statutory categories. Median citations per thousand words are 6.01 for flagged complaints, 4.40 for unflagged post-AI complaints, and 3.98 before the cutoff; the author treats these as legal form, not legal quality. Among terminated post-AI cases, dismissal rates are 61.1% versus 53.6%, and termination before an answer is 47.8% versus 39.0%. Plaintiff-win rates among clearly coded judgments are 6.4% versus 8.4%, a nonsignificant difference based on 47 flagged and 333 unflagged cases. Screening and comprehension explanations draw on lawyer-gatekeeping studies, sycophancy research, OpenAI's 2025 rollback, procedural authorities, and AI-citation sanctions cases. Nippon Life's chatbot-related account is expressly identified as allegations in pending litigation. The polish penalty relies on ghostwriting and legally trained pro se precedents plus research on impressions and fluency, not a direct study of judicial treatment of AI-drafted complaints. Reform benefits and costs are proposed predictions, not evaluated interventions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical claims concern the period through FY2025 after ChatGPT's November 30, 2022 release; causal mechanisms and institutional reforms are qualified explanations and prospective predictions.
pts.d: FY2023-Q1 is treated as a transition quarter. The pooled post-cutoff pro se share of 16.94% is distinct from the final-quarter FY2025 figure of 22.30%. The author explicitly calls the evidence associational rather than causal and acknowledges pending-case censoring. Complaint-level findings mainly concern freely drafted complaints in two focal categories, rather than every federal civil case or all AI assistance. AI flags detect visible drafting signatures, not verified individual use, and may miss brainstorming, translation, research, or drafting in the litigant's own words. The absence of a higher win rate is a per-case conclusion: more filings could still yield more favorable outcomes in absolute terms. The author acknowledges that traditional lawyer screening also reflects economics and ability to pay rather than merit alone; sycophancy varies by model and context. The severed-authorship account is strongest where litigants adopt output without comprehension, and weakens where they learn from AI and draft independently. The pure polish penalty is explicitly a prediction. Prospective reforms have no fixed implementation deadline and must respect limits on court intake authority: coercive statutory screening applies to in forma pauperis cases, while the fee-paid majority generally requires an advisory rather than exclusionary front door. Reserving adverse decisions for humans is defended on legitimacy grounds even if future models become more accurate.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects center on unrepresented civil litigants, courts, defendants, and the professionals who supply screening and assistance, with uneven gains across litigant groups and case types.
pts.d: Self-represented plaintiffs gain inexpensive drafting capacity and participation but may still lack factual pleading, comprehension, verification capacity, and remedies. Flagged complaints disproportionately involve first-observed filers: 79.4% versus 70.2%, where 'first-time' means first observed primary-plaintiff name in the FY2018–FY2025 identity-linked sample, not necessarily first litigation ever. A higher name-inferred female share is treated as suggestive. Financially constrained litigants are not disproportionately represented in flagged complaints: fee-waiver rates of 27.3% versus 24.4% do not differ significantly, and the overall pro se fee-waiver share declined. The surge varies by case category and geography; Civil Rights and Other Statutory cases are focal, while Social Security and Immigration pro se shares decline. Judges, staff, and defendants bear screening work previously performed privately or avoided when claims were never filed. Lawyers' gatekeeping role is partly bypassed, but the author does not infer equivalent displacement of represented legal work. Proposed reforms would expand or create roles for pro se staff attorneys, magistrate judges, neutral intake evaluators, self-help centers, and AI-oriented legal aid, while automation handles ministerial tasks. General-purpose AI providers are described as outside the established professional-duty structure; the author suggests targeting sycophancy without banning drafting assistance. Broader procedural institutions may also be affected wherever rules assume costly legal production or human authorship.
